clue.text: Really pretty futile, but not quite a disaster

indicators.note: a disaster is a wreck, so the letters before it are thrown into a new order
not quite the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: Someone sighs that something is very nearly ruined but still fairly nice to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims BUT to BU; 'disaster' then rearranges FUTILE + BU + A. 'Really pretty' looks like 'quite', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something really pretty is lovely to look at: a straight synonym for very attractive.

clue.text: Wood put up by way of workshop

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up makes it read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: as in 'used as a doorstop', meaning in the role of or by way of
a lab is a place where work and experiments are done

explanation.surface: Timber is hoisted onto a shelf as you pass through the workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns AS LAB into the light timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Balsa is a very light tropical timber used by model makers, an example of the class.

clue.text: Coppola's apocalyptic concoction

indicators.note: something apocalyptic is utterly destructive, so the director's name is smashed and rebuilt; a nod to his film Apocalypse Now

explanation.surface: Francis Ford Coppola, director of Apocalypse Now, mixes a disastrous drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apocalyptic' rearranges COPPOLA.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcopop is a sweet, ready-mixed alcoholic drink, a kind of mixed-up beverage.

clue.text: Put mark on spaceship driver's travel permits

parts.note: to tick is to put a check mark against something
ET, the alien of the film, flew a spaceship; with the 's he gives ET'S

explanation.surface: Someone stamps the travel documents of a space pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: ET is Spielberg's extra-terrestrial; his possessive supplies the last three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tickets are the documents that let you travel on a train, bus or plane.

clue.text: Overindulgent pasta chef ends up so?

definitions.text: Overindulgent pasta chef ends up so?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the picked letters are read bottom to top
the final letters of the three words are taken

explanation.surface: A chef who eats too much of their own pasta ends up looking a certain way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends' picks T, A, F from the three words; 'up' reverses them. The whole clue also describes the outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: Overeating rich pasta would leave a cook carrying excess weight, i.e. plump.

clue.text: Short boy climbing steps and ropes

indicators.note: short of its last letter, so the word for boy is clipped

parts.note: a lad is a boy

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a stair can mean a flight of steps

explanation.surface: A small lad climbs the stairs and the ropes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' clips LAD to LA; 'climbing' turns STAIR into RIATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Lariats are lassos, long ropes with a running noose used by cowboys.

clue.text: Willing to empty garbage outside before noon

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
emptying a word takes out its insides, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: a.m. is the morning, before noon

explanation.surface: Someone is ready to take the rubbish out before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to empty' leaves G and E of garbage, which go 'outside' AM.
explanation.definitionFit: To be game for something is to be ready and willing to try it.

clue.text: Nearly lose one's sight encountering first of Sauron's Orcs

indicators.note: nearly the whole phrase, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to go blind is to lose one's sight

indicators.note: the opening letter of the name is taken

explanation.surface: A Tolkien character almost goes blind on meeting Sauron's orc army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' trims GO BLIND to GOBLIN; S comes from 'first of Sauron's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Orcs and goblins are the same race of brutish creatures in Tolkien's fiction.

clue.text: Noise of crazy pub still poses challenge

indicators.note: the noise a phrase makes is how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: manic means crazy and an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A rowdy pub's din somehow becomes a test of keeping still.
explanation.walkthrough: MANIC INN, said quickly, sounds like the answer. The definition alludes to the Mannequin Challenge, a 2016 online craze in which people froze in place on camera.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mannequin Challenge was a viral video craze in which participants held still poses like shop dummies.

clue.text: Ominous sign of cricketer about to miss century

indicators.note: the cricketer goes about, i.e. around, the other pieces

parts.note: a bat is a batsman
to lack something is to miss it
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A batsman about to fall short of a hundred is a bad omen.
explanation.definitionFit: A black cat crossing your path is a traditional omen, bad luck in some superstitions.

clue.text: Garden birds beginning to repopulate old ditches

indicators.note: the beginning of the word, its first letter, is taken

parts.note: to bin something is to throw it away, as to ditch it

explanation.surface: Birds start returning to fill neglected old trenches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ditches' looks like a noun (trenches) but is a verb: bins.
explanation.definitionFit: Robins are small red-breasted birds familiar in British gardens.

clue.text: Power for Thatcher's second government? It'll mean sorrow for some

indicators.note: one thing put for another means it replaces it

parts.note: Maggie was Margaret Thatcher's nickname
the second G in the name; G is short for government
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A question about granting power to a second Thatcher administration, which some would mourn.
explanation.walkthrough: Of Maggie's two Gs, the second is swapped for P. The definition alludes to the counting rhyme 'One for sorrow, two for joy'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme, seeing a single black-and-white bird of this kind foretells sorrow.

clue.text: Puff the magic dragon, say, resides with a surrealist

indicators.note: surrealist art distorts reality, so these letters are distorted into a new order

explanation.surface: The song's dragon lives alongside a Dali-style painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrealist' rearranges RESIDES + A.
explanation.definitionFit: In the song, the dragon 'lived by the sea', making it a resident of the coast.

clue.text: Picture including a horse with earliest of street urchins

indicators.note: the first piece holds the next ones within it

parts.note: to picture something is to see it in the mind
gee-gee, GG, is a childish word for a horse

indicators.note: the earliest letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Imagine a horse among the urchins of the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'urchins' looks like street children, but sea eggs are sea urchins.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea eggs is another name for sea urchins, spiny marine creatures.

clue.text: Magic target: to split housework

parts.note: split into its two halves, house gives HO and work gives OP

explanation.surface: A conjurer aims at sharing the household chores.
explanation.walkthrough: HO and OP are standard abbreviations for house and work (opus). 'Magic' is the Orlando Magic basketball team, whose target is the basket.
explanation.definitionFit: A basketball team such as the Orlando Magic aims the ball at the ring and net.

clue.text: Claiming to be single, he told fanciful lies inside

indicators.note: the anagram lies inside the word for single

parts.note: one is single

indicators.note: fanciful means made up, so the letters are reinvented

explanation.surface: A benefit fraudster pretends to be unattached and tells tall tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Claiming' here means claiming benefit, not asserting; 'fanciful' and 'lies inside' are two separate signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone claiming unemployment benefit in Britain is said to be on the dole.

clue.text: Was changing partners in order to get partners for life?

indicators.note: the word is changed, its letters put in a new order

parts.note: North and South are bridge partners

explanation.surface: Someone swapped spouses to find a lifelong mate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges WAS; N and S sit opposite each other at the bridge table.
explanation.definitionFit: These birds famously pair with one mate for their whole lives.

clue.text: Driver's wrong to ignore debts

definitions.note: read as 'driver is'; the definition is the noun driver

indicators.note: ignoring part means leaving it out of the word

parts.note: spurious means false or wrong
IOUs are written acknowledgements of debts

explanation.surface: A motorist is accused of wrongly ignoring what they owe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to ignore' takes IOUS out of SPURIOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A spur is a goad or incentive that drives someone on.

clue.text: Lay on predominantly male party

indicators.note: most of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: to stage an event is to lay it on

explanation.surface: Organising a party attended mostly by men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'predominantly' trims STAGE to its first four letters. 'predominantly male' looks like one phrase, but it is split.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag party or stag do is a groom's night out with male friends.

clue.text: Granny on vacation charges for twerks?

indicators.note: a vacated word is emptied, leaving its outer letters

parts.note: rates are charges or fees

explanation.surface: A grandmother on holiday charges fees for her dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' empties GRANNY to GY.
explanation.definitionFit: Twerking involves rotating the hips, so it is a form of whirling motion, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Darwin's ship loses prow, the result of almost hitting an albatross?

definitions.text: the result of almost hitting an albatross?

indicators.note: a ship's prow is its front, so the first letter goes

parts.note: Charles Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle

explanation.surface: Darwin's ship is damaged after nearly striking a seabird.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf an albatross is three under par and an eagle two under, so just missing the first gives the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf score of two under par is one stroke worse than three under, its next-best term.

clue.text: Outspoken cockney intellectual, one raised to show scepticism

indicators.note: spoken in a cockney accent, which drops the H

parts.note: a highbrow is an intellectual

explanation.surface: A frank Londoner who is also an intellectual shows doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: A cockney (East Londoner) drops the initial H, so 'highbrow' comes out as ''ighbrow'.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising one brow over the eye is the classic gesture of doubt.

clue.text: Part of parliament — it legislates to grant authority

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A legislature passes laws to confer powers.
explanation.definitionFit: To entitle someone is to give them a right or authority to do something.

clue.text: Puts on half loved tubular scarf back to front

indicators.note: the word is turned round to read in reverse
the pair of loves in the scarf word is cut by half, down to a single one

parts.note: a snood is a tube of knitted fabric worn as a scarf or hood
read as love doubled: two O letters, each O being love (nil)

explanation.surface: Someone pulls on a tube scarf the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: SNOOD holds two O letters (love = nil); 'half' cuts that pair to one, leaving SNOD, and 'back to front' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: To don clothing is to put it on.

clue.text: Government department used banks for swindle

parts.note: DEFRA is the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

indicators.note: a word's banks are its outer letters, as a river's banks are its edges

explanation.surface: A ministry used banks to cheat people.
explanation.definitionFit: To defraud is to cheat someone out of money, a synonym for swindle.

clue.text: Judges locking up Queen's best friends?

indicators.note: the judges lock up, i.e. enclose, the queen

parts.note: triers are those who try cases
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen

explanation.surface: Magistrates imprison the monarch's closest companions.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on dogs as man's best friend; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog is called man's best friend, and these small dogs are one breed group of them.

clue.text: Sweet beverage initially taken for cold

indicators.note: one letter taken for another replaces it

parts.note: coffee is a hot drink
C is the tap abbreviation for cold

indicators.note: the initial letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A sugary drink is first mistaken for a chilled one.
explanation.walkthrough: The T of 'taken' replaces the C of COFFEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffee is a chewy confection of boiled sugar and butter, an example of a sweet.

clue.text: Pennies oddly lacking — the writer's nemesis

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are missing, leaving the even ones

parts.note: the writer of the clue would say 'my'

explanation.surface: Lack of money is the author's arch foe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly lacking' leaves E, N, E from Pennies.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is an arch-rival or foe.

clue.text: Expert at tables and he's a natural speller

definitions.meaning: a skilled player of snooker or pool, games played on tables
Harry, the boy wizard, casts spells by instinct

explanation.surface: A table expert who also happens to spell well.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pots balls at snooker, and the surname of J K Rowling's young wizard.

clue.text: Get actor performing as rural labourer perhaps

indicators.note: the letters perform, acting out a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An actor is cast as a farmhand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'performing' rearranges GET ACTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A cottager is a person living in a cottage, historically a farm worker.

clue.text: Payment terms for school members

definitions.meaning: cash on delivery, a condition of payment
fish swimming together form a school; these are one such fish

explanation.surface: Fees at a school, read two ways.
explanation.definitionFit: COD abbreviates cash on delivery and is a fish found in schools.

clue.text: Building society engaging phone company workers

indicators.note: the first piece engages, i.e. holds, the second

parts.note: BS is the abbreviation for a building society, a British mutual savings bank
EE is a British mobile network operator

explanation.surface: A building society hires staff from a telecoms firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Worker bees are the sterile females that do the hive's labour.

clue.text: Midweek match time sees Ding become 'born leader of snooker'

indicators.note: one part becomes another, so it is replaced

parts.note: a match is a marriage, and its day is the wedding day
taken as written; Ding Junhui is a Chinese snooker player
nee marks a maiden name, meaning born

indicators.note: the leading letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A midweek fixture sees snooker player Ding Junhui hailed as a natural champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' looks like a sports fixture but is a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: This weekday falls in the middle of the working week.
